title: Tihove
author: Vho-Mashudu
desc: Samp boiled two and a half hours, beans cooked alongside, and crushed raw peanuts stirred through to bind them — the Vatsonga dish where the groundnut is what holds the whole thing together.
longDesc: Tihove is the Tsonga cousin of Venda's tshidzimba and Tswana dikgobe: grain, legume and pounded nut, cooked long and eaten with a thin stew. The traditional tool is a wooden mortar that crushes the nuts to a fine powder, and the reason is structural rather than decorative — the groundnut is what makes the samp and the beans hold to one another instead of sitting in the bowl as two separate things. A simpler version leaves the beans out entirely and is still tihove.
ingredients: 1 cup dried beans — sugar beans or cowpeas
1 litre hot water, plus 2 to 3 litres more during cooking
2.5 ml (1/2 tsp) salt, or to taste
equipment: A second saucepan, for the beans
Wooden mortar and pestle, or a food processor
steps: Wash the samp and the beans separately. Soak them 15 minutes and skim off any debris that floats.
Boil the samp in 1 litre of water, adding more as it is absorbed, for about 2 1/2 hours until soft. Taste it often rather than trusting the clock.
Season the samp with about half a teaspoon of salt.
At the same time, boil the beans in 2 cups of water until tender.
Season the beans lightly with salt and set them aside.
Crush the raw peanuts to a fine powder in a mortar, or grind them in a processor.
Combine the cooked samp, the beans and the crushed nuts and stir thoroughly — the groundnuts are what bind the samp and the beans together.
Simmer over very low heat for 30 minutes.
Serve alongside beef stew with a thin gravy.
chefTips: Soaking the samp in hot water overnight cuts a good chunk off the two and a half hours.
Cook the beans in their own pot. Beans in with the samp go to mush long before the samp is soft.
Taste the samp rather than timing it. Samp varies enormously by brand and by age, and two and a half hours is a starting estimate.

The published version of this recipe calls for beans in four of its steps but leaves them out of the ingredient list altogether. A cup of sugar beans or cowpeas is the sensible reading, and the beanless version is also traditional.
Crushed, not blended. A fine powder binds; a paste just makes it claggy.
commonMistakes: Cooking the beans and samp in one pot.
Under-cooking the samp, which stays chalky rather than creamy.
Letting the water run dry — keep topping it up through the whole two and a half hours.
Serving it without a gravy. It is meant to be eaten with something wet.
servedWith: Beef stew with a thin gravy
reheating: Warm with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Samp, beans and peanuts together form a complete protein.
High in fibre and slow-release carbohydrate.
Groundnuts supply monounsaturated fat, niacin and magnesium.
Contains peanuts — not suitable for anyone with a nut allergy.
culturalNote: Tsonga food is the least written-down of South Africa's major cuisines, and tihove is one of very few Vatsonga dishes with a properly published recipe. The pattern it shares with tshidzimba and dikgobe — grain, legume, pounded groundnut — runs right across the north of the country and into Mozambique and Zimbabwe, irrespective of language.
